doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Color tones, altered chords and writing for male and female voices
summary: Favorite R&B chord extensions and how he voices strings differently behind men and women.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Here's an odd question: do you have a favorite dissonance that you employ on occasion? Or color tones that work well with strings?

Well in R&B I would say that they would only be the sevenths and the ninths or the elevenths. You know? I mean so it's like you're always looking for that magic note that goes well with the vocal, not per se with — even though the chord has to allow you to do that, but I think the altered chords, which we used to call, at Curtis they were altered chords okay? But they're not any more in life called that. But I think they're part of what the appetite right now is still in R&B.

If you're writing for a woman as opposed to a man, is there a tendency — well let me rephrase — a guy's voice is going to be an octave lower than a woman singing the same melody. Does it affect the range that you write in, depending?

Absolutely. Yeah I mean the tendency is to give him that space, whereas on a female voice I have all the bottom that I can use and on a male voice I tend to maybe like spread it out a little bit more so that I don't get in his way. But sometimes I do. Sometimes I like to get in the way and rub a little bit. You know? I think that's part of it. And I even think like you know like a lot of the hip hop records that I've done, you know I like doing that. Because I don't think if I bring in high things, sometimes it's inappropriate for the record. So I'm always looking for a way of saying something within the context of the record more than the context of male or female vocals.
